questions.clue: Short single-stranded DNA sequences that define where DNA polymerase begins synthesis.
questions.explain: Primers (~18–22 nt) anneal to template DNA and provide a 3'-OH for extension.

questions.clue: In the basic Tm formula (4°C × G/C + 2°C × A/T), GC pairs contribute more because they form this many hydrogen bonds.
questions.explain: G-C pairs form 3 hydrogen bonds vs. 2 for A-T, making them more stable and raising Tm.

questions.clue: When annealing primers to your template strand, what matters more: The amount of time the annealing step takes, or the temperature during the annealing step?
questions.explain: The temperature needed to anneal your primers to the template is critical, and varies based on primer length and GC content. Annealing time is typically short, only 15-30 seconds, and the length of this step usually doesn’t impact generation of the PCR product.

questions.clue: Besides percent G-C content, another aspect of ideal primer design is to include at least this many G-C nucleotides in last 5 bases at the 3' end of your primer
questions.explain: If there’s less than 3 G-C nucleotides in the last 5 bases at the 3’ end of primers, this may cause the 3’ end of the primer to bind poorly to the target strand, decreasing annealing efficiency. It may also cause the DNA polymerase to fall off (transiently detach) during the extension step. Both of these outcomes would impair the amount of PCR product you generate!

questions.clue: This artifact occurs when primers anneal to each other rather than the template, consuming primer and reducing yield.
questions.explain: Primer dimers form via complementary 3' ends and are amplified by Taq, appearing as a small band near the bottom of a gel.

questions.clue: The PCR step at ~95°C that separates double-stranded DNA into single strands.
questions.explain: Denaturation breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, producing single-stranded templates.

questions.clue: The PCR step where primers bind to their complementary sequences on single-stranded template.
questions.explain: Annealing occurs 5°C below the primer Tm, typically 50–65°C, allowing specific primer binding.

questions.clue: Extension time per kilobase of product for Taq polymerase (in minutes).
questions.explain: Taq extends at ~1 min/kb at 72°C; High-fidelity polymerases are often slower (~2 min/kb).

questions.clue: Typical number of PCR cycles for routine amplification from genomic DNA.
questions.explain: 25–35 cycles amplify a single copy ~10⁷–10¹⁰ fold; exceeding 35 cycles increases non-specific bands. (However, if you're trying to amplify a difficult DNA template, you may go up to 40 cycles! ... And end up with a lot of primer dimer in your PCR product!)

questions.clue: The optional final step (5–10 min at 72°C) ensures all partial extension products are fully completed.
questions.explain: The final extension fills in any incomplete strands before storage.

questions.clue: These four nucleotides included a PCR reaction mix are the building blocks incorporated by DNA polymerase during PCR extension.
questions.explain: dNTPs (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP) provide the nucleotides for new strand synthesis.

questions.clue: What is the thermostable DNA polymerase originally isolated from Thermus aquaticus, used in many PCR reactions?
questions.explain: Taq survives repeated 95°C denaturation; it lacks 3'→5' proofreading and adds A-overhangs.

questions.clue: When should enzymes be added to your PCR reaction mix?
questions.explain: Enzymes like Taq polymerase need optimal buffer conditions to maintain their enzymatic activity. Additionally, adding your enzymes last prevents the PCR reaction from starting prematurely.

questions.clue: After 10 PCR cycles starting from a single template copy, the theoretical number of copies produced.
questions.explain: PCR doubles copies each cycle: 2¹⁰ = 1024.

questions.clue: If PCR efficiency is 95%, each cycle multiplies copies by this decimal value.
questions.explain: Efficiency E means each cycle multiplies by (1 + E/100); 95% → 1.95.

questions.clue: Average molecular weight of one base pair in daltons, used in DNA copy number calculations.
questions.explain: Each bp ~660 Da; divide DNA mass (in g) by (bp count × 660) to get moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.clue: A standard curve slope of −3.32 in qPCR corresponds to this PCR efficiency (in %).
questions.explain: Efficiency = (10^(−1/slope) − 1) × 100; slope −3.322 = 100% efficiency.

questions.clue: In a serial dilution standard curve, each 10-fold dilution step should shift the Ct by approximately this many cycles at 100% efficiency.
questions.explain: log₂(10) ≈ 3.32 cycles per decade; this is the mathematical basis for the −3.32 slope at perfect efficiency.

questions.clue: Multiple non-specific bands on a gel suggest the annealing temperature should be adjusted in this direction.
questions.explain: Raising the annealing temperature increases primer specificity, eliminating non-target bands.

questions.clue: Where does primer dimer appear on a gel relative to other DNA bands?
questions.explain: Primer dimer is when your primer anneals to itself. Because it is formed by the binding of short-length primers to itself, it’s small size means will migrate faster and lower on an electrophoretic gel than your larger (longer) PCR products. Therefore, it frequently appears as a band on the lower portion of your gel.

questions.clue: On a gel, what would you include to determine your reaction worked properly and produced the desired PCR product?
acceptedAnswers: positive control lane negative control lane
questions.explain: Without proper controls, you have no way of known if the PCR product you just made is actually your target, or a random off-target product that happens to be around the same size. By including a known positive control lane, you can be more confident that the bands generated by your PCR reaction are your genuine target. Negative controls are essential to ensure your bands aren’t the result of some off-target or unexpected target amplifying. Plus, it’s an empirical test that gives you confidence in your primer’s specificity.

questions.clue: No band at all despite good template quality most often indicates a problem with this component of the master mix.
questions.explain: Degraded, misprimed, or incorrectly designed primers are the most common cause of no-amplification failures.

questions.clue: Amplicon contamination that produces false positives in subsequent runs is called this type of contamination.
questions.explain: Carryover contamination is prevented by physical separation of pre/post-PCR areas, use of a PCR clean hood to prepare reactions, UV decontamination between runs, and thorough cleaning of workspaces with a DNA denaturing solution.

questions.clue: When using Inverse PCR to linearize your vector, what must you treat your product with to avoid high background?
questions.explain: Dpn1 selectively cuts methylated DNA. An Inverse PCR reaction should be treated with Dpn1 to remove any remaining template plasmid from the product. Otherwise, the leftover template plasmid will show up as background in gel electrophoresis or sanger sequencing.

questions.clue:
Name the three enzymes required for Gibson assembly
(DO NOT include commas in your answer!)
acceptedAnswers: dna polymerase dna ligase 5 prime to 3 prime exonuclease

questions.clue: What ratio of insert DNA to plasmid is ideal to achieve efficient assembly of your desired plasmid?
questions.explain: Ideally, you want twice as much molar amount of insert to the amount of target vector in your Gibson assembly reaction.

questions.clue: In what direction does T5 Exonuclease digest DNA?
questions.explain: T5 Exonuclease digests one strand of DNA from the 5’ end in the 3’ direction. It leaves behind a single strand of DNA referred to as the 3’ overhang on the complimentary strand to the DNA strand it digested.

questions.clue: What enzyme is used in the final step of Gibson assembly and what is its function? (DO NOT use commas in your answer!)
acceptedAnswers: dna ligase adds nucleotides to gaps
dna ligase fills nucleotides into gaps
questions.explain: After the overlapping DNA fragments anneal together, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to extend the 3’ ends of the overhangs. However, a gap will remain between the existing DNA and the portion added by the DNA polymerase. In the final step of Gibson assembly, DNA ligase will seal the nicks between the new and old DNA fragments, covalently linking all the DNA fragments together.

questions.clue: What’s the optimal amount of low-complexity plasmid DNA to add to your PCR reaction?
questions.explain: Amplifying a complex DNA template, such as whole genomic DNA, may require more input DNA to be added to your reaction for adequate replication.

questions.clue: The divalent cation cofactor required by all thermostable polymerases; typical concentration in PCR is 1.5–2.5 mM.
questions.explain: Mg²⁺ is essential for polymerase catalysis and primer annealing; too much or too little reduces specificity.

finalQuestion.clue: All plasmids that are used for cloning contain what three features?
finalQuestion.answer: Origin of replication antibiotic resistance gene and multiple cloning site
acceptedAnswers: Origin of replication antibiotic resistance gene and polylinker
finalQuestion.explain: The origin of replication (ORI) site is where initiation proteins bind to start DNA replication in bacteria. Antibiotic resistance genes are used to select for bacteria successfully transformed with your plasmid on antibiotic containing agar plates. Finally, the multiple cloning site (MCS, or polylinker) is the region that contains multiple DNA sequences that can be targeted different restriction enzymes to allow the addition of your desired DNA insert.
